quote: In wiefern ist die Methode des arithmetisch geometrischen Mittels ein Beispiel für die De- finition einer transcendenten Function durch Annäherung [-dals-] Grenze von algebraischen Functionen?
english: To what extent is the method of the arithmetic-geometric mean an example of the definition of a transcendental function by approximation as a limit of algebraic functions?
topic: The page asks in what sense the arithmetic-geometric mean method exemplifies defining a transcendental function as a limit of algebraic functions, then states the conditions under which a pair of real functions of four real variables defines a regular analytic function of two complex variables, and begins a statement about single-valued functions rational in y.

triage.modern_statement: This is a conceptual or teaching question, not an open research problem. In the AGM iteration a_{n+1}=(a_n+b_n)/2, b_{n+1}=sqrt(a_n b_n), every a_n and b_n is an algebraic function of the starting values (a,b), built from repeated means and square roots. Both sequences converge to a common limit M(a,b), and that limit is transcendental: M(1,sqrt(1-k^2)) = pi/(2K(k)), where K is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind (Gauss). So the AGM is a standard example of a transcendental function defined as a uniform limit of a sequence of algebraic functions. Hilbert seems to be asking in what precise sense this holds: algebraic approximants, convergence and its domain (rapid quadratic convergence), and the transcendence of the limit, as a model for building transcendental functions.
triage.answered_by: The content was already settled before Hilbert wrote this. Gauss linked the AGM to the lemniscate and elliptic integrals (diary entry of 30 May 1799; later work c. 1799–1818). Lagrange and Legendre found the algorithm independently. A modern standard account is D. A. Cox, 'The arithmetic-geometric mean of Gauss', L'Enseignement Mathématique 30 (1984), 275–330. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: The AGM was discovered independently by Lagrange, Legendre and Gauss, with Gauss going into the most detail. Cox's 1984 paper is the standard reference.
Cox, 'The arithmetic-geometric mean of Gauss', L'Enseignement Math. 30 (1984), 275-330. It discusses Gauss's diary entry of May 30, 1799 linking the AGM to the lemniscate.
In 1799 Gauss found that the AGM connects the lemniscate's half-circumference with pi. In other words, the limit of the algebraic iteration is a transcendental (elliptic) quantity.
The Landen/AGM recurrence gives a numerical method for evaluating elliptic integrals.

triage.why: This diary note reads like a reflective or lecture-planning question about a classical example. It does not pose an unsolved problem. It was already answered by Gauss's theory of the AGM and complete elliptic integrals. The approximants a_n and b_n are algebraic, and their common limit is pi/(2K), which is transcendental. Work on the AGM continues today (high-precision computation, periods of genus 1 and 2 curves), but nothing there is an open version of this question. My sources confirm the AGM–elliptic integral link. None of them comments on Hilbert's note itself, so how I read his intent is my own interpretation.
